Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A misty autumn birch grove with a leaf-covered path running back into the fog

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

22 stepsCanvas: 16 x 12 inFocal point: The two big leaning birches left of center, against the sunlit gold haze, with the path opening beside them Light: A low sun at the upper left, behind the trees: the left of the wood glows gold, the right side and the pines sit in cool blue shade, and the trunks are lit on their left sides.How this lesson was made

Before you start

You are painting a misty autumn birch grove, with a leaf-covered path running back into the fog. The two big leaning birches are the heart of it, pale bark against a glowing gold haze. Keep the far things soft and the near things bold, and the mist will do the rest.

The light

A low sun shines through the wood from behind the trees, so the gold bushes and leaves nearest it glow while the pines sit in cool blue shade. The birches and the rock catch that sun on the side facing it and fall into shadow away from it.

What this painting teaches

  • Dabbing (steps 6, 7, 8, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22). Dabbing is tapping with the tip of a dry brush, so the paint lands as separate dots that turn into leaves. It builds the bushes, the leaves overhead and the fallen leaves, always dark first, then middle, then the sunlit ones. Keep the brush dry and lightly loaded, or the dots turn into blobs.
  • Dry brush (steps 3, 10, 15, 17). Dry brush is a nearly dry brush skimmed lightly so the paint catches only the canvas texture. It makes the mist, the shadows on the path, and the soft shade and light on the birch bark. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.
  • Thick to thin (steps 2, 14, 16). Thick to thin is pressing the brush's full width, then easing onto its edge so the mark tapers. It pulls the far trunks and the birches, wide at the foot and narrow as they rise, and makes the short dark bark marks.

The way there

First comes the misty background, the farthest thing, so the depth is there before anything solid. Then the near woods: the pines and the golden bushes. Next the ground with its path and the mossy rock. The birches, the subject, go on over all of it, and then the gold leaves overhead and the fallen leaves go over the trunks. The brightest sunlit leaves come last. The first layers stop where the ground will cover them, so bare canvas showing early on is expected.

This lesson skips about half a canvas of painting that later layers would cover.

Placing shapes with a transfer outline optional

The transfer outline (optional)

The outlines of the main shapes, on a grid of quarters: 1 The mossy rock; 2 The birches. On your 16 x 12 in canvas the grid lines are 4 in apart across and 3 in apart down. Before the stage that starts one, you can lightly chalk its outline on the canvas, measuring from the edges with a ruler.

Getting started

The other basics are in the steps where they matter.

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.

Paint thickness and how much is on the brush

Not checked yet

  • Each step's Load line says two different things. How thick the paint is, and how much of it is on the brush. Creamy paint can be a full load or a light one.

How thick the paint is

How much is on the brush

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.
If something goes wrong not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.

The misty background 3 steps

This stage lays the soft, misty fog that everything else stands in.

Where: Inside the outlined area. Its top is at the top edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 15 1/2 in wide and 8 in tall.

STEP 1 OF 22 · The misty background, 1 of 3

Blend the misty glow

  • Start: Start at the top edge near the left edge with Birch gray-white and a little Golden yellow, and work toward the right edge.
  • Strokes: Make short criss-cross X strokes, picking up Haze blue as you move right, overlapping so the colors melt together.
  • Where the paint sits: Most of the glow ends up soft Haze blue. Keep a faint warm streak of Golden yellow and Birch gray-white low on the left side of the glow, where the low sun shines through.
  • Leave: The layer stops short at a loose, uneven lower edge about 6 1/4 in from the top edge, not a ruled line. The rest of the canvas stays bare until step 4.
  • Stop when: Stop when the top of the canvas is a soft, cool fog with a faint warm glow, and the criss-cross marks still show.

Stroke: X stroke how to do it, not checked yet

X stroke also called criss-cross, slip-slap

Not checked yet

With. flat

Load. One or two colors on the brush. How much of each is on it controls the blend.

Motion. Short strokes that cross each other in two directions, like overlapping X shapes.

What it leaves. A soft, slightly textured blended fill with visible criss-cross marks.

Then. For a smooth, even gradient, go over it while wet with lighter, longer side-to-side strokes. Or leave it as texture.

Fill with crossing strokes

STEP 2 OF 22 · The misty background, 2 of 3

Pull the far misty trunks

  • First: Let the glow dry first, so the trunks stay crisp.
  • Start: Start with one thin trunk whose left side is about 3 1/2 in from the left edge, beginning low in the glow.
  • Strokes: Press the brush's full width at the trunk's foot, then turn onto the edge and lighten as you pull up toward the top edge, so it tapers thin.
  • Where the paint sits: That trunk runs almost the whole height of the glow. Add a short, soft dab of trunk about 2 in from the left edge, and one short piece about 11 in from the left edge.
  • Leave: Leave the soft fog showing all round these few marks. The rest of the canvas stays bare until step 4.
  • Stop when: Stop with one clear thin trunk and two small soft marks, faint and far away in the fog, with no bark marks.

Basics: Making a color lighter or darker

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.
Stroke: Thick to thin how to do it, not checked yet

Thick to thin

Not checked yet

With. flat; angle

Motion. Press the full width of the brush for the thick part, then turn onto its edge or tip and lighten the pressure. With an angle brush, the lighter you press, the thinner the line.

What it leaves. A line that starts wide and tapers to a point.

Then. Add a few thinner offshoots with a liner.

Good for. branches, grass

Wide, then onto the edge

STEP 3 OF 22 · The misty background, 3 of 3

Dry-brush the mist down the path

  • First: The far trunks must be dry before you skim over them.
  • Start: Start low in the middle of the misty glow, where the bottoms of the far trunks fade into the fog.
  • Strokes: With a nearly dry brush, skim lightly side to side, barely touching the canvas, so the paint catches only the texture.
  • Where the paint sits: Keep it to the lowest part of the glow in the middle, over the feet of the far trunks, where the path will later vanish into fog.
  • Leave: Leave the trunks' upper parts and the rest of the glow untouched. The bare canvas stays bare until step 4.
  • Stop when: Stop while it is barely visible: a faint veil that softens the trunk bottoms. If you can see a clear patch of paint, it is too much.

Dry brush

Not checked yet

With. flat; old stiff flat (catches the canvas weave best)

Load. Wiped nearly dry. Only the tip goes in the paint, and no water on the brush. It should feel dry and hard to apply.

Motion. Light pressure, skimming the surface.

What it leaves. Feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.

Then. Build up in several light passes.

Good for. cloud highlights, grass, wood and fences, highlights on round things

The pines and the golden bushes 5 steps

This stage adds the dark pines and the glowing golden bushes in front of the fog.

Where: Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 3/4 in from the top edge, and its right side is at the right edge; it's about 6 in wide and 6 1/2 in tall.

STEP 4 OF 22 · The pines and the golden bushes, 1 of 5

Stamp the dark pines

  • First: Let the glow dry first.
  • Start: Start at the tip of the tallest pine, near the top edge, about 13 in from the left edge, then do a shorter pine each side.
  • Strokes: Stamp with the middle tips of the fan, working down each pine in a zigzag. Press harder as you go down, so each pine widens toward the ground.
  • Where the paint sits: The pines run from about 9 3/4 in from the left edge to the right edge. Leave small gaps where the fog shows through.
  • Leave: The layer stops short at a loose, uneven lower edge about 8 3/4 in from the top edge, going onto bare canvas there. The rest of the canvas stays bare until step 9.
  • Stop when: Stop when three soft, dark, ragged pines stand over the far trunks, with small fog gaps and no light on them.

Stroke: Fan brush tapping how to do it, not checked yet

Fan brush tapping

Not checked yet

With. fan

Load. Thin paint. Stroke the brush on the palette until the bristles fan out.

Motion. Stamp only the tips, using the middle of the fan, not the side bristles. For a shape that widens, work from the top down in a zigzag and press harder as you go down. Short strokes in different directions make a rough texture.

What it leaves. Clusters of fine, needle-like marks, light at the top and heavier where pressed.

Then. If the top is too heavy, add a few fine lines with a small round instead of more fan marks.

Good for. a pine, from the top down in a zigzag, grass, with short strokes in different directions

Tap, then zigzag down

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • Heavy, clumpy marks. The paint is too thick, the bristles are clumped, or you stamped with the side. Thin the paint a little, spread the fan, and stamp with the middle tips.

Try it on scrap paper first.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 5 OF 22 · The pines and the golden bushes, 2 of 5

Tap light on the pines' left side

  • First: The dark pines must be dry first.
  • Start: Start on the left edge of the tallest pine's upper branches, about 13 in from the left edge, where the sun from the upper left reaches.
  • As in step 4: Same fan tapping as the dark pines, but lighter, and only on the sunlit branch edges and the small fog gaps.
  • Strokes: Stamp short taps with the middle tips of the fan, working down each pine in a zigzag, angling the taps down and out like branch ends.
  • Where the paint sits: Put the light on the sun-facing left edges of the branches on each of the three pines, and into the small fog gaps, which it fills.
  • Leave: Leave the dark showing between the light taps and on the shaded right parts of each pine. The rest of the canvas stays bare until step 9.
  • Stop when: Stop when the pines have soft gray-green light along their left sides with dark showing beneath. They should still read as mostly dark.

STEP 6 OF 22 · The pines and the golden bushes, 3 of 5

Dab the dark of the golden bushes

  • First: The pines must be dry first.
  • Start: Start at the left edge of the canvas with the big bush, its top about 4 1/4 in from the top edge.
  • Strokes: Tap with the tip of a nearly dry brush, building a rounded mound of loose dots.
  • Where the paint sits: The bush reaches about halfway across the canvas. Then tap a low band across the foot of the pines, out to the right edge.
  • Leave: Leave small gaps between the dots. The layer stops at a loose, uneven lower edge about 8 3/4 in from the top edge. The rest of the canvas stays bare until step 9.
  • Stop when: Stop when a broken brownish mound sits at the left and a low band sits along the foot of the pines, with gaps still showing.

Stroke: Dabbing how to do it, not checked yet

Dabbing also called stippling

Not checked yet

With. round (the tip, for small dots); old stiff brush (for rough patches); a sponge, for soft patches

Load. A light load. No water on the brush: a wet one makes blobs.

Motion. Tap with the tip of the brush. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.

What it leaves. Dots or dappled patches that get more solid the more you tap.

Then. Tap a lighter mix on the lit side, leaving the darker taps showing underneath.

Good for. foliage, with an old stiff brush, small dots, with the tip of a round

Tap, don't stroke

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • Blobs instead of dots. The brush is too wet or holds too much paint. Wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.
  • A patch went too solid. Tap over it with a lighter or darker mix to break it up.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 7 OF 22 · The pines and the golden bushes, 4 of 5

Dab the middle gold on the bushes

  • First: Let the darker bush dots from step 6 dry first.
  • Start: Start on the top of the big bush at the left, near the left edge of the canvas.
  • As in step 6: Same tapping as the dark dots, now with a brighter paint that covers most of the big bush.
  • Strokes: Tap with the tip of a dry brush, working across the mound and down, tapping more where you want it solid.
  • Where the paint sits: Cover most of the big bush and fill its gaps, since it is lit by the sun. Then tap a single row of dots along the band at the foot of the pines.
  • Leave: Leave the darker dots from step 6 showing low on the big bush. The rest of the canvas stays bare until step 9.
  • Stop when: Stop when the big bush reads as a bright warm mound with darker dots low down, and the band at the pines has a bright row along it.

Not checked yet

  • Between steps, the paint underneath should be dry to the touch. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  • Painting into half-dry paint drags it up and turns it gooey and muddy.
  • Thick paint can feel dry on top and still be wet inside. Give thick areas longer.
  • Fine lines and light colors over dark especially need a dry layer underneath.
Basics: One light direction

One light direction

Not checked yet

  • Pick where the light comes from and put every highlight on that side.
  • Each thing is built the same way: the whole shape in a darker or middle value, a lighter value on the side facing the light, then the lightest on a small area at the very edge. Each covers less than the one before.

STEP 8 OF 22 · The pines and the golden bushes, 5 of 5

Tap the sunlit tops of the bushes

  • First: Let the gold dots dry first, so the pale taps stay clean.
  • Start: Start on the top of the big bush, about 2 1/4 in from the left edge, where it faces the low sun.
  • As in step 6: Same tapping again, but only a few pale dots on the bush's sunlit crown.
  • Strokes: Tap lightly with just the tip of a dry brush, a few dots at a time, along the top of the mound.

  • Stop when: Stop when the big bush has a pale sunlit crown, gold through the middle and darker at the bottom.

STEP 9 OF 22 · The ground and the rock, 1 of 5

Lay in the ground and the path

  • First: Let the bushes dry first.
  • Start: Start at the bottom edge of the canvas and work up to the loose lower edge of the bushes and pines, about 7 in from the top edge.
  • Strokes: Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right across the canvas, row after row, with Rust orange.
  • Where the paint sits: Lay a strip of Path tan from the bottom edge near the middle of the canvas, narrowing as it goes back to the fog. Make the front darker and rougher, the back smoother.
  • Leave: Cover all the bare canvas, and slightly overlap the lower edge of the bushes and pines. Leave the fog showing where the path meets it.
  • Stop when: Stop when the whole lower canvas is warm orange ground with a pale path running back into the fog. No shadows or rock yet.

STEP 11 OF 22 · The ground and the rock, 3 of 5

Build the rock from pieces

  • First: Let the ground dry first.

Building from pieces

Not checked yet

Motion. Start with one simple shape (an oval, a circle, or a rectangle). Then add the rest in curved pieces on each side, like ( ), smaller toward the edges.

What it leaves. A shape made of distinct curved segments with small gaps or overlaps between them.

Then. Soften where the pieces meet only if the shape should look smooth; otherwise leave the pieces showing.

Good for. shaped objects (a pumpkin is a center oval, then curved pieces on each side like ( ))

STEP 14 OF 22 · The birches, 1 of 4

Pull the pale birch trunks

  • First: Everything must be dry, since the trunks go over all of it.
  • Start: Start with the big leaning trunk whose left side is about 1/2 in from the left edge, at its foot on the ground.
  • As in step 2: The same thick-to-thin pull as the far trunk, with a bigger brush and much wider trunks pulled from the ground up.
  • Strokes: Press the brush's full width at the foot and pull up to the top edge, easing the pressure so the trunk narrows as it rises.
  • Where the paint sits: The two big trunks lean right as they rise. Add a thin trunk at the left edge, a slim one about 7 3/4 in from the left edge, and two near the right edge.
  • Leave: Leave the bushes, pines and ground showing between the six trunks.
  • Stop when: Stop when six tall, flat pale trunks stand on the ground, the two big ones widest, with no shading or marks.

STEP 15 OF 22 · The birches, 2 of 4

STEP 16 OF 22 · The birches, 3 of 4

Lay the dark bark marks

  • First: Let the gray-brown patches dry first.
  • Start: Start at the foot of the big trunk whose left side is about 1/4 in from the left edge.

  • Strokes: Press the brush's edge flat for a short dark dash across the trunk, then lift so it tapers out. Stack the dashes up each trunk.

Before starting

Subject: A misty autumn birch grove with a leaf-covered path running into fog

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: Nothing in the image is outside the scene.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 16 x 12 in, landscape

Done: crop

Left out: about a ninth of the photo, thin strips at the sides

Why: The default size closest to the photo's shape; the path, the big birches and the hazy light stay.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: Textures of hundreds of items: yes (twigs, canopy leaves, leaf litter; busy measured 55.8%). Detail inside big shapes: yes (bark). Tiny separate things: no. More parts than 8: about 8.

Changed: Twigs and thin branches removed; only the main birches kept plus a few pale trunks in the fog; far trunks merged into blue-gray haze; the dark trees right of the path one soft blue-green mass; canopy and bushes as loose golden dabs; leaf litter as loose horizontal ochre and burnt-orange dabs; bark as bold dark dashes; the rock one gray-green shape.

Why: Every step is copied from the finish. Fine texture fell from 55.8% to 13.1%; what is left is the leaf dabs and bark marks the lesson teaches. No redo.

Fine texture measured: the photo 55.8%, the beginner version 13.1%, the finish 0.2% of the canvas

A misty autumn birch grove with a leaf-covered path running into fog. What matters is the depth: fog behind, golden bushes, then the pale leaning birches in front and the bright leaves. What's hard is the leaves, which have to be dabbed in passes, and the bark marks.

Subject: A misty autumn birch grove with a leaf-covered path running back into the fog
Focal point: The two big leaning birches left of center, against the sunlit gold haze, with the path opening beside them
Light: A low sun at the upper left, behind the trees: the left of the wood glows gold, the right side and the pines sit in cool blue shade, and the trunks are lit on their left sides.

What it saw, back to front

  1. The misty glow behind the wood
  2. The far misty trunks
  3. The mist down the path
  4. The leaf-covered ground and path
  5. The mossy rock
  6. The birches
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

The only technique with version 2 keys, and the picture paints back to front on white canvas.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner.yaml)

It has no version 2 keys, so the pipeline can't plan with it.

How the paint recipes were worked out20 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Where Claude drew diagrams2 steps, free

Read each step as a first-time painter with only its picture and words. Steps that make a shape appear whole, or whose marks follow a structure, get a diagram; the rest are fills, repeated marks, or small shapes the words place. The writer wrote to the pictures where they differ from the plan, so no line was changed.

  • Step 11: Build the rock from pieces beginner check

    Noticed: A shaped object appears whole in one step.

    Pieces: A low oval, a dome over it, softened into one shape with a flat bottom.

  • Step 14: Pull the pale birch trunks beginner check

    Noticed: How a leaning trunk starts and tapers isn't clear from the picture.

    Pieces: Press the full brush at the foot, then ease off and lean as you pull up.

What the reviewer caught9 notes

A second Claude, with fresh eyes and none of this reasoning, compared each picture with its neighbors and the finish. It gets two rounds of fixes, then stops; anything still off is flagged on its step. A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

  • Finish check The view came out a little closer than the photo: the birches are larger and the slim far-left birch sits at the left edge.
  • Text check: paint Step 1: The paint called Mist white keeps the plan's rough color: the pictures don't show it where the plan lays it. (left: build-steps' note; a new plan and chain would be needed.)
  • Text check: chain Step 2: Most of the far misty trunks are already in step 1's fog; this step adds only one trunk and two small marks. (left: the image model removed only a few trunks in two more tries.)
  • Text check: chain Step 2: The far trunks step also paints the pointed top of the dark misty pine left of center, which belongs to the background. (left: the chain's checker still marks it after two more tries.)
  • Text check: chain Step 3: The mist step changes almost nothing a painter would see: the image model left the mist down the path in place. (left: two more tries changed nothing.)
  • Text check: paint Step 13: The paint called Moss gray light was measured as a warm tan (#d3ac6d), not gray. (left: renaming it would render part of the chain again; build-steps' note.)
  • Text check: words Step 13: Every sentence of its stop line failed the fact check, so the page leaves that line off. (left: check-text --final took it out.)
  • Text check: chain Step 20: Some fallen leaves are already on the ground before this step (about 3% of the canvas), where the image model didn't take them out. (left: erase lists it after two more tries.)
  • Text check: paint Step 20: The paint called Leaf gray was measured as a brown (#6b4d3c), not gray. (left: renaming it would render part of the chain again; build-steps' note.)

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • Helpers, and what each was given (all Opus, fresh contexts). Plan writer: v3/plan-brief.md, the lesson folder, the photo and the technique file; at C3 it was sent check's merge (Glow cream into Birch gray-white) with make only this change, which rendered 10 chain units again. Chain checker: v3/chain-check.md and chain/looks, two redo rounds. Lesson writer: words/lesson (brief.md, feedback.md, arc-brief.md). Steps 0, 1 and E were done in the session that started the run.
  • Made for #299's gate: one chain, built twice. This side with build-steps --stops.

Known problems

Where the pictures aren't quite right. Paint it the way the step says and use the picture as a guide.

  • Step 1, Blend the misty glow: The paint called Mist white keeps the plan's rough color: the pictures don't show it where the plan lays it.
  • Step 2, Pull the far misty trunks: Most of the far misty trunks are already in step 1's fog; this step adds only one trunk and two small marks.
  • Step 2, Pull the far misty trunks: The far trunks step also paints the pointed top of the dark misty pine left of center, which belongs to the background.
  • Step 3, Dry-brush the mist down the path: The mist step changes almost nothing a painter would see: the image model left the mist down the path in place.
  • Step 13, Light the rock's top left: The paint called Moss gray light was measured as a warm tan (#d3ac6d), not gray.
  • Step 13, Light the rock's top left: Every sentence of its stop line failed the fact check, so the page leaves that line off.
  • Step 20, Dab the dark fallen leaves: Some fallen leaves are already on the ground before this step (about 3% of the canvas), where the image model didn't take them out.
  • Step 20, Dab the dark fallen leaves: The paint called Leaf gray was measured as a brown (#6b4d3c), not gray.
